attemptsAndFailures.what: Live catalog loop, first run before absorbing the CloudIdentity dependency
attemptsAndFailures.outcome: failed as expected: HTTP 403 action is not authorized for createComputePlan
attemptsAndFailures.reason: CloudIdentity's generated policy carried no resource_catalog action. This is the evidence that the dependency was genuinely missing and that the check is not a stub.

attemptsAndFailures.what: Live catalog loop against the absorbed policy, first attempts
attemptsAndFailures.outcome: failed three times with distinct real causes, each repaired in source
attemptsAndFailures.reason: (1) the BFF named the plan id as the authorization resource while the owner named only the catalog kind, so CloudIdentity refused the authorization-context continuation as a different resource — the BFF now names the same resource the owner does; (2) the test driver passed the actor id where the session reference belongs; (3) the cross-owner read assertion expected a neighbour schema in another database.

proven: A real platform-administrator session reaches the Console BFF catalog surface and the owner persists an approved compute plan, an approved storage plan, a retention policy version and a refund policy version in the owner's own PostgreSQL database, and the same owner reads the created policy versions back.

The generated CloudIdentity policy admits the catalog actions for the contract's actors: 10 platform-admin actions with platform scope and 2 member reads with tenant scope return ALLOWED under real session validation; a tenant administrator and a member are refused the platform actions.
A refused action writes nothing: an administrator-only command from a tenant administrator leaves zero rows.
A member may read the customer catalog list and is refused the administrator policy list.
Retiring a storage plan changes the owner's availability projection to retired, and pricing a retired plan pair is refused with FailedPrecondition at the owner boundary.

Idempotent replay returns the originally stored plan, a conflicting body under the same key is refused with 409, and a lost-response retry converges on the original row instead of creating a second one.
The owner's runtime login cannot read a neighbour schema in its own database (PostgreSQL permission denied) and does not carry another owner's schema.
The full local gate passes on the frozen revision with every required PostgreSQL package at zero skips, including the new services/resource-catalog lane.
notProven: Quoting does not exist: CreateQuote, GetQuote and the Workspace-facing AcceptQuote are unimplemented, so nothing prices a deploy, resize or renew request. This change does not close pricing or a Local deployment loop.

No money-bearing price policy version travels the BFF wire. The shared public JSON codec resolves properties by protobuf JSON name while the canonical contract spells those amounts computeMonthlyUSDMicros / storageMonthlyUSDMicros / productMonthlyUSDMicros, so a contract-shaped body is rejected (decode: unknown publisher property CreatePricePolicyRequest.productMonthlyUSDMicros) and an encoded version emits the protobuf spelling with a bare number instead of the required decimal string. Observed in this repository, evidence below; the owner command itself is verified at its typed boundary only.

The contract declares 200 for the two plan-availability actions; the shared authenticated route boundary currently returns 201 because the action is not in its explicit 200 exemption list. Handed to the BFF serial integrator; not claimed as contract-conformant here.

The shared route boundary's own catalog wiring line (registerCatalogRoutes in apps/console-bff/internal/httpapi/server.go) is the BFF integrator's file and is handed over rather than written here, so no process-served catalog route is claimed.

The Ledger DomainInbox still accepts only tenant-scoped build and capability producers, so the platform-scoped catalog.policy_changed.v1 delivery stays pending. The producer records and retries it; extending the consumer is Ledger's write set, and the event is not claimed end-to-end.
No Workspace subscription, original order, provider resource or Local-Docker reference was touched or verified, and no real charge, purchase or provider resource exists.
No Candidate, Product Release, deployment or Instance qualification was performed, and no production endpoint, database or service was accessed.
